character_facts: The speaker addressing 'milady' claims to have learned love and is determined to save the girl.
A speaker associated with 'my poet' wants the girl to survive so he can raise her.
The avian-faced attendants are talkative and concerned with clan naming rules.
Steelhead is directly associated with the surgical brain-transplant procedure.

A higher-status female addressee implied by the term 'milady'
A speaker referring to the child as the offspring of 'my poet'

continuity_links: This page centers on the birth and emergency survival of a girl child tied to the Castaka lineage.
The operation appears to establish the girl's survival through extreme surgical intervention, likely important to her later identity or role.
dialogue_meaning: One speaker has become emotionally invested and insists the baby girl must live.
Another speaker sees the child as a source of renewed purpose tied to someone called 'my poet'.
Some attendants object because preserving a girl conflicts with a lineage rule attached to the Castaka name.
A superior figure silences the attendants and orders them to stop interrupting.
Medical staff deliver grim updates about the twins' condition and the girl's malformed skull.
Narration boxes describe the separation and brain-transplant procedure step by step.
locations: An industrial/mechanical interior surrounding the operating table
lore_facts: Within the Castaka clan, a son is said to be the one who can bear the family name.
A caesarean birth is performed in this setting.
The newborn twins are conjoined at the hip.
The twins possess only one brain between them.
The girl is described as having a hollow skull.
Steelhead performs or leads a brain transplant into the girl.
The girl's skull is reconstructed with a replacement crown after surgery.
plot_events: A male speaker vows that a girl child will survive.
Another speaker frames the child as the offspring of 'my poet' and says she will give him a reason to live and raise her.
Observers argue over the consequences of saving a girl, noting that only sons can bear the Castaka name.
An operation report states that the caesarean succeeded but produced conjoined twins joined at the hip.
A further report reveals the twins share only one brain and that the girl's skull is hollow.
The surgery proceeds to separate the conjoined twins.
The shared brain is transplanted into the girl's head.
The girl's skull crown is replaced, concluding the operation.

visual_summary: A blue-toned, industrial surgical chamber is shown in fragmented panels. Mechanical figures and birdlike attendants speak around an operating table. A childbirth by caesarean is reported as successful, but the newborn twins are conjoined and share only one brain. The page then shows a grim surgical procedure in which the twins are separated and the shared brain is transplanted into the girl, whose skull is mechanically reconstructed.
